title: The Boston Tea Party
subtitle: A cold December night, three ships, and ninety thousand pounds of tea in the water.
description: An A2 reading and listening text on the Boston Tea Party of 1773: the tax on tea, the protest in the harbour, and what Britain did next.
source: authored for this site; no source document
passage: On the night of 16 December 1773, about a hundred men walked down to the harbour in Boston. It was cold and dark, and they were going to destroy a very large amount of tea.
The problem had started years before. Britain needed money after a long war, so it put taxes on things the American colonists bought.
The colonists did not like paying taxes to a parliament in London, because they had nobody there to speak for them. They stopped buying British goods, and Britain removed most of the taxes.
But one tax stayed: the tax on tea. For London it was a small tax. For the colonists it was a question of principle.

In 1773 a new law gave one British company, the East India Company, the right to sell tea in America more cheaply than anybody else. Many colonists saw a trap. If they bought the cheap tea, they accepted the tax.
Three ships with tea arrived in Boston. The colonists asked the governor to send the ships back to England. He said no.
So the men went down to the harbour. Some of them had put blankets around their shoulders and paint on their faces, because they did not want anybody to recognise them.
They worked for about three hours. They opened 342 big boxes of tea and threw everything into the water. They broke nothing else, and they hurt nobody.
In the morning, tea was floating all over the harbour. People say the water smelled of tea for days.
Britain was furious. Parliament closed the port of Boston and sent soldiers. Instead of ending the protest, this brought the thirteen colonies together, and eighteen months later the war began.

images.alt: A coloured print of men on a moored ship throwing boxes of tea into the harbour while a crowd watches from the quay
images.caption: *The Destruction of Tea at Boston Harbor* — Nathaniel Currier, 1846. Printed seventy years afterwards, with a crowd on the quay that the written accounts do not entirely support.

items.prompt: When did the Boston Tea Party happen?
Why did Britain put taxes on the colonies?
options: It needed money after a long war
items.explanation: Britain needed money after a long war.

items.prompt: Which tax stayed after the others were removed?
items.explanation: The tax on tea — small in money, large in principle.

items.prompt: Why did many colonists not want the cheap tea?
options: They did not like the taste
Buying it meant accepting the tax
items.explanation: They saw a trap: if they bought the cheap tea, they accepted the tax with it.

items.prompt: What did the men do at the harbour?
options: They threw the tea into the water
items.explanation: They opened 342 boxes and threw the tea into the water. They broke nothing else.

items.prompt: What did Britain do after the protest?
options: It closed the port of Boston and sent soldiers
items.explanation: It closed the port and sent soldiers — which brought the colonies together instead of dividing them.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide if each sentence is true or false.

items.statement: The men hurt the sailors on the ships.
items.explanation: False — “They broke nothing else, and they hurt nobody.”

items.statement: The governor sent the ships back to England.
items.explanation: False — the colonists asked him to, and he said no.
True — they used blankets and paint so that nobody would recognise them.

items.statement: The protest took about three hours.
items.explanation: True — they worked for about three hours.

items.statement: The war started on the same night.
items.explanation: False — the war began about eighteen months later.

exercises.title: Vocabulary in Use
exercises.instructions: Choose the best word for each sentence.

items.prompt: A place where ships stop next to a city is a ___.
When you are extremely angry, you are ___.
items.explanation: Furious. Parliament was furious about the tea.

items.prompt: Things that people buy and sell are ___.
items.explanation: Goods. The colonists stopped buying British goods.

items.prompt: To stay on the top of water is to ___.
items.explanation: To float. The tea floated all over the harbour.

items.prompt: A strong idea about what is right is a ___.
items.explanation: A principle. The tax was small; the principle was not.

exercises.title: Put the Story Together
exercises.instructions: Match each event with the reason or result.

pairs.left: Britain needs money after a war
pairs.right: it puts taxes on the colonies

pairs.left: The colonists stop buying British goods
pairs.right: Britain removes most of the taxes

pairs.left: The governor will not send the ships back

pairs.right: Britain closes the port of Boston

items.explanation: Each event in this story is an answer to the one before it. That is how the war arrived: nobody planned it in 1773.

discussion: Was destroying the tea a good way to protest? What else could the colonists have done?
Have you ever stopped buying something because you did not agree with a company or a government?
Britain punished the whole city of Boston. Why can punishing a group make a problem bigger?
